scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4659: The campus network keeps going slow for us in bursts
-- transfers crawl for a bit, then recover, then crawl again, and it is like
that in waves for everyone, not just one desk. A couple of the more
technical people here are certain about it: the main router -- they call it
router0 -- is dropping our packets. I wouldn't know a packet if I saw one,
and I don't have to; they would. Something is losing our traffic and it is
on your side. Check it and sort it out today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router0 has ip_forward enabled, its interfaces
  are up, and traffic transiting router0 between segments arrives with 0% loss; there
  is no drop-inducing ACL or forwarding fault. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of packet loss on router0 that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- router0 dropping/forwarding
traffic incorrectly -- is NOT reproducible: a ping across router0 (between two
segments it connects) completes with 0% loss, router0 has ip_forward enabled, its
interfaces are up, ripd is running, and there is no drop-inducing ACL.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: router0 is forwarding correctly and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces a path transiting
router0, finds 0% loss, checks router0's ip_forward, interfaces, and any filters, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" router0 dropping packets -- blaming an ACL,
forwarding, or load to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
**Affected component:** No subsystem, daemon, interface, or policy was found to be misconfigured or failed.

**Mechanism:** The helpdesk ticket describes intermittent wave-pattern throughput degradation affecting all campus users, with router0 suspected as the drop point. This symptom pattern would most plausibly be caused by one of four mechanisms: (1) a traffic-control qdisc (tbf or netem) injecting a rate limit or artificial delay on a router interface, (2) a stress or flood tool consuming CPU or link bandwidth on a device, (3) repeated link carrier flaps causing brief outages, or (4) routing instability causing periodic reconvergence.

**Localization:** Every device in the lab (30 total, 43 interfaces inspected) was covered. Router0's upstream and downstream interfaces were included in the tc_snapshot and l2_snapshot sweeps. No shaping qdisc (tbf, netem) was found on any interface — all 43 interfaces carry the default fq_codel profile. Pressure_sweep found no stress-tool processes, CPU spikes, or socket-count anomalies on any device including router0. DHCP/link history found no carrier transitions or network-down events on any device. Infra_sweep found no ACL drop rules, no static ARP poisoning, and no addressing or gateway divergence.

**Root cause:** The reported intermittent campus-wide slowdowns have no detectable mechanism or historical trace in the current live lab state; the fault claim is unconfirmed.

**Fix:** No corrective action is warranted. The network is operating normally. If the slowness recurs, capture concurrent iperf throughput measurements and check `tc -s qdisc show` on router0 at the time of the reported degradation to catch any transient qdisc or resource event that was not present during this diagnostic window.
